analysis.one_liner: Phases out feeding livestock antibiotics that are also used to treat people.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without ever getting a vote, despite 78 House cosponsors and support from major medical groups.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required drug makers to prove that antibiotics approved for livestock do not fuel antibiotic resistance in humans, and would have withdrawn approval for routine, non-medical uses—like growth promotion—of drugs that matter in human medicine. It would also have limited dosing whole barns of healthy animals as a substitute for cleaner living conditions. Four out of five pounds of antibiotics sold in the U.S. go to food animals, so the bill targeted the largest single use of drugs that keep common infections treatable.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who may someday need an antibiotic to work—people with pneumonia, skin infections, food poisoning, or any bacterial illness—because the bill aimed to keep existing drugs effective. It also would have reduced antibiotic-resistant bacteria on retail meat, which federal monitoring already finds and which Consumer Reports documented in pork [S3]. It would have protected farm workers and rural residents living near large animal operations from resistant bacteria [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone who might ever need an antibiotic

how_it_helps.text: Requires drug makers to demonstrate a reasonable certainty of no harm to human health from resistance before a medically important antibiotic can be used nontherapeutically in food animals, and directs HHS to withdraw existing approvals within two years unless that showing is made [S2].

Prohibits routine dosing of healthy animals in feed and water for growth promotion, feed efficiency, or disease prevention, and limits nonroutine disease control to the shortest duration, at barn or pen level, on the fewest animals necessary [S2].

The bill's findings cite federal data that 80% of antibacterial drugs sold in the U.S. in 2010 went to food animals rather than people, and cite the Danish experience showing a similar ban cut resistance sharply with only a modest production-cost increase and little change in animal health [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Livestock producers and animal-drug manufacturers, who would lose the ability to use human-important antibiotics routinely to speed growth and compensate for crowded conditions. Consumers could see modestly higher meat prices; the Danish precedent cited in the bill found only a modest cost increase [S3].

drawbacks.text: Restricting routine antibiotic use could raise meat production costs and require farmers to change how they house and manage animals; the bill's own findings put the Danish cost increase at only modest, but U.S. confinement systems differ from Danish ones [S3].

The disease-control exception still allows barn- or pen-level dosing of healthy animals when disease is present or likely, which animal-health advocates could argue leaves room for continued group treatment in large operations [S2].

It places a heavy evidentiary job on the FDA—reassessing decades-old animal-drug approvals within a two-year window, a deadline the agency has historically struggled to meet even under court order [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit—keeping existing antibiotics effective against pneumonia, food poisoning, and other common infections—is large and falls on everyone, while the costs fall on a specific industry and are estimated as modest based on the Danish precedent the bill cites. The two-year deadline for re-reviewing old drug approvals was ambitious and could have been difficult to execute, but that is a design quibble, not a reason the underlying public-health case fails.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee in March 2013 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2015 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Louise Slaughter of New York introduced the bill on March 14, 2013, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, then to its Subcommittee on Health the next day [S5].

The bill drew 78 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and the bill text lists the American Medical Association, the American Public Health Association, and more than 400 health, consumer, and agricultural organizations among its supporters [S4][S3].

No further action was ever taken: the action history ends with the subcommittee referral, meaning the committee never scheduled a markup or sent the bill to the floor before the 113th Congress adjourned [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Livestock producers and animal-drug manufacturers kept the status quo: routine antibiotic use in food animals continued unchanged, with only FDA's voluntary guidance in place. The general public got no protection against the growth of antibiotic-resistant bacteria that the bill's findings documented [S3][S5].

for.name: Louise Slaughter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through introduction; a trained microbiologist who had sponsored similar legislation in prior Congresses.

for.name: American Medical Association and 400+ health, consumer, and farm organizations
for.what_they_did: Endorsed legislation to phase out nontherapeutic antibiotic use in farm animals, as listed in the bill's findings.

against.name: Fred Upton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; after subcommittee referral in March 2013, no action of any kind followed for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Livestock industry and animal-drug manufacturers
against.role: Industries whose routine antibiotic use the bill would have restricted
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on nontherapeutic antibiotic use in food animals, keeping the debate off the committee agenda; the bill's own findings show the scale at stake—13.5 million kilograms of antibacterial drugs sold for food animals in 2010 versus 3.3 million for human use.

sides.party_line_note: All 78 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; the Republican-chaired committee that controlled the bill's fate took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would have ended routine feeding of human-important antibiotics for growth promotion and disease prevention, a practice USDA surveys show on roughly 84% of swine farms and cattle feedlots. The Danish precedent cited in the bill showed resistance fell sharply with only a modest production-cost increase, but U.S. producers would have faced adjustment costs, which consumers could partly absorb through meat prices.

With 13.5 million kilograms of antibacterial drugs sold for food animals in 2010—four times the human-use total—the nontherapeutic livestock market was the larger side of their antibiotic sales, and the bill would have phased it out unless safety from resistance was proven.
